title: Nouns, Number, and Gender
summary: The plural in -లు, and the two genders Telugu makes where European languages make three — masculine and non-masculine, with no feminine as such, and a line between them that falls in one place for the singular and in quite another for the plural.

rules.heading: The Plural in -లు
rules.statement: The plural of a Telugu noun is made by adding **-లు** to it. There is one plural ending and not several, and the difficulty lies not in the ending but in what the stem does before it.

examples.note: abbāyi → abbāyilu; the stem is untouched

rules.heading: What the Stem Does Before -లు
rules.statement: Many nouns change before the plural ending, and the changes fall into a few regular kinds. A noun in **-ం** replaces it with a long vowel; a noun in **-లు** or **-డు** turns that consonant into **-ళ్ళు**.

paradigms.caption: Stem changes before -లు

cells: the anusvāra gives way to a long vowel

rows.label: -లు → -ళ్ళు
cells: l becomes a doubled retroflex ḷ

rows.label: -డు → -డ్లు
cells: the ḍ is kept and l added beneath it

rows.label: -ి → -ులు
cells: a vowel comes in before the ending

paradigms.footnote: The commonest of all is the first: nouns in -ం, which are very numerous, all make their plural in -ాలు.

rules.heading: Two Genders, Not Three
rules.statement: Telugu distinguishes two genders, masculine and non-masculine, and has no feminine gender as such. A noun naming a male person is masculine; a noun naming a woman, an animal, or a thing is non-masculine.

examples.gloss: she / it — non-masculine, whichever word is used

footnotes: The older grammars call the two genders మహత్ (mahat) and అమహత్ (amahat), Sanskrit terms for "the great" and "the not-great"; Krishnamurti and Gwynn use masculine and non-masculine instead, and this course follows them.

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, p. 190.
sources.note: Source for the మహత్ / అమహత్ terminology.

rules.heading: The Line Moves Between Singular and Plural
rules.statement: Which gender a noun takes depends on its number as well as on what it names: the boundary between masculine and non-masculine falls in one place for the singular and in another for the plural. A noun that stands alone as non-masculine can become masculine once there is more than one of it.

paradigms.caption: The moving line
paradigms.footnote: A woman is non-masculine alone and masculine once she is one of several people.

examples.gloss: one girl → non-masculine అది; girls → masculine వాళ్ళు

rules.heading: The Singular Masculine: Male Persons Only
rules.statement: In the singular, the masculine gender contains male persons and nothing else. The demonstratives **వాడు**, **అతను**, and **ఆయన** all refer to a man, and the verb takes the ending **-డు**.

paradigms.caption: The singular masculine
paradigms.footnote: The three demonstratives differ from one another in the respect they show, not in gender; that grading is set out later in this course.

examples.note: అతను is masculine, and refers only to a man

rules.heading: The Singular Non-Masculine: Everything Else
rules.statement: Everything else in the singular — a woman, an animal, a stone — is non-masculine, and shares one pronoun, **అది**, and one verb ending, **-ది**. A woman is thereby grouped with the dog and the stone.

paradigms.caption: The singular non-masculine

rows.label: non-masculine
cells: a woman, an animal, a thing

paradigms.footnote: ఆమె and ఆవిడ are also used of a woman; the grammar treats her as non-masculine regardless of which of the three words is chosen.

examples.note: అది of a thing, non-masculine and unremarkable

rules.heading: A Child Is Non-Masculine
rules.statement: **పిల్ల** and **బిడ్డ**, the ordinary words for a child, are non-masculine regardless of the child's sex. Both take **అది** and the verb ending **-ది**, exactly as a woman or a thing does.

examples.target: ఇది ఒక పిల్ల. అది మంచి పిల్ల.
examples.gloss: This is a child. It/She is a good child.
examples.note: అది agrees with పిల్ల whether the child is a boy or a girl

rules.heading: అది of a Woman Is Impolite
rules.statement: అది of a woman is impolite; the ordinary words are **ఆమె** or **ఆవిడ**. The verb ending stays **-ది** whichever word is chosen, since the politer words are still grammatically non-masculine.

examples.note: ఆమె is the ordinary, respectful word

rules.heading: The Plural Masculine: All Persons Together
rules.statement: In the plural, the masculine gender widens to include every person, male or female. All persons take **వాళ్ళు** and the verb ending **-రు**, so that a woman who was non-masculine alone becomes masculine among others.

examples.gloss: The girls are here. They are my friends.
examples.note: girls are people, so masculine in the plural — వాళ్ళు, never అవి

examples.gloss: Boys and girls are here — they.
examples.note: both sexes share one plural pronoun once there is more than one person

rules.heading: The Sexes, Alone and Together
rules.statement: The sexes are distinguished when a person stands alone, and are not distinguished once several stand together. This single fact governs the pronoun, the demonstrative, and the verb ending alike.

examples.target: ఆమె నా అమ్మ. అమ్మాయిలు నా స్నేహితులు — వాళ్ళు.
examples.roman: āme nā amma. ammāyilu nā snēhitulu — vāḷḷu.
examples.gloss: She is my mother. The girls are my friends — they.
examples.note: one woman is non-masculine; women together are masculine — the line has moved

rules.heading: The Plural Non-Masculine: Animals and Things
rules.statement: Animals and things remain non-masculine in the plural, and take **అవి** and the verb ending **-యి**. They are counted with the ordinary numerals, never with the numerals reserved for people.

examples.gloss: The dogs are there. They are big.
examples.note: dogs are not people, so non-masculine — అవి
counted like any non-masculine noun, with the same numeral things take

vocabulary.gloss: he (very informal; rude of a stranger)

drills.explanation: -లు is added and the stem is untouched. This is the simplest of the plural classes.
A noun in -ం gives up its anusvāra for a long vowel before -లు: *pustakaṃ → pustakālu*. Nouns of this shape are very numerous, so the class is worth meeting first.

drills.stem: In the **singular**, which of these belongs to the **masculine** gender?
drills.explanation: In the singular the masculine gender holds male human beings and nothing else. A woman is grammatically non-masculine, grouped with the dog and the book.

drills.stem: **అమ్మాయిలు ఇక్కడ. ___ నా స్నేహితులు.** Which pronoun fills the blank?
drills.explanation: Girls are people, and in the plural every person is masculine — so *వాళ్ళు*, not *అవి*. *అది* and *ఆమె* are singular.

drills.stem: Which of these are correct plurals?
drills.explanation: The last is wrong: a noun in -ం gives up the anusvāra, making *పుస్తకాలు*. The other three show three different stem-classes, all regular.

drills.stem: Which statements about the Telugu gender system are correct?
options: In the singular, a woman is grammatically non-masculine.
In the plural, a woman is grammatically masculine.
The line between the genders is drawn the same way in both numbers.
Telugu has no feminine gender as such.
drills.explanation: The line is drawn in one place in the singular and another in the plural — that is the whole peculiarity. Telugu makes only masculine and non-masculine; there is no third, feminine, category.

drills.stem: **ఆమె** is the ordinary, respectful word for *she*. What does that change about her grammatical gender?
options: It makes her masculine in the singular.
Nothing: the verb still treats her as non-masculine.
It makes her masculine in the plural only.
It removes her from the gender system.
drills.explanation: The word chosen and the grammatical gender are two different things. Whichever pronoun is used, the singular verb ending for a woman is the non-masculine one — which is why *అది* of a woman is merely impolite, and not ungrammatical.

drills.stem: Of **a man, a woman, a dog, and a book**, how many are masculine in the **singular**?
drills.explanation: One — the man. In the singular the masculine gender holds male human beings only. Answering two counts the woman, which is exactly the assumption a European learner brings and must give up.

drills.stem: Of **a boy, a girl, a cow, and a chair**, how many are masculine in the **plural**?
drills.explanation: Two — the boy and the girl, who are together masculine once they are plural. The cow and the chair stay non-masculine whatever their number.

drills.stem: **కుక్కలు అక్కడ. ___ పెద్దవి.** Which pronoun fills the blank?
drills.explanation: Dogs are not people, so in the plural they remain non-masculine — *అవి*. *వాళ్ళు* is only for persons.

drills.stem: Which of these sentences choose the **right** third-person pronoun?
drills.explanation: The second is wrong: dogs take *అవి*, not *వాళ్ళు*. Girls take *వాళ్ళు*; books take *అవి*; one woman takes *ఆమె* — each by gender and number.

drills.stem: Compare **ఆమె నా అమ్మ** with **అమ్మాయిలు నా స్నేహితులు — వాళ్ళు**. What has moved?
options: Nothing: a woman is non-masculine in both numbers.
The line of gender: one woman is non-masculine, women together are masculine.
The pronoun is optional in the plural.
drills.explanation: That is the whole surprise of the moving line: the sexes are distinguished when alone and not when together. The same person who is *ఆమె* in the singular is one of *వాళ్ళు* in the plural.

drills.stem: In **ఆమె నా అమ్మ. అతను నా అన్న. వాళ్ళు నా స్నేహితులు. అవి నా పుస్తకాలు.** how many **different** third-person pronouns appear?
drills.explanation: Four: *ఆమె*, *అతను*, *వాళ్ళు*, *అవి* — singular non-masculine, singular masculine, plural masculine, plural non-masculine. Telugu will not let one *they* cover the last two.

drills.stem: **ఇది ఒక పిల్ల. ___ మంచి పిల్ల.** Which pronoun fills the blank, whether the child is a boy or a girl?
drills.explanation: పిల్ల is non-masculine regardless of the child's sex, so *అది* agrees with it. *అతను*, *వాడు* and *ఆయన* are all masculine, and reserved for a male person.

drills.stem: Which of these words can refer to a man?
drills.explanation: వాడు, అతను and ఆయన are all masculine demonstratives, differing only in respect. అది is non-masculine and never refers to a man.

drills.stem: Match each pronoun with its gender and number. One label in Column II fits none of them.
drills.explanation: అతను is singular masculine, ఆమె singular non-masculine, వాళ్ళు plural masculine, and అవి plural non-masculine. The second option swaps the two singulars; the third swaps the two plurals — the two commonest agreement errors. "The near-series demonstrative" fits none of the four, which are all of the far series.

drills.title: ఇక్కడ ఎవరు?
drills.passage: ఇక్కడ అబ్బాయిలు, అమ్మాయిలు. వాళ్ళు నా స్నేహితులు. ఇక్కడ ఒక పిల్ల. అది మంచి పిల్ల. అక్కడ కుక్కలు, చెట్లు. అవి పెద్దవి. ఇది నా ఇల్లు. అక్కడ రెండు ఇళ్ళు. ఆమె నా అమ్మ. అతను నా అన్న.
drills.romanization: ikkaḍa abbāyilu, ammāyilu. vāḷḷu nā snēhitulu. ikkaḍa oka pilla. adi mañci pilla. akkaḍa kukkalu, ceṭlu. avi peddavi. idi nā illu. akkaḍa reṇḍu iḷḷu. āme nā amma. atanu nā anna.
drills.translation: Here are boys and girls. They are my friends. Here is a child. It/She is a good child. There are dogs and trees. They are big. This is my house. There are two houses. She is my mother. He is my elder brother.

glossary.పెద్దవి: big (the plural form of పెద్ద used as a predicate)

questions.explanation: *అక్కడ కుక్కలు, చెట్లు* — the dogs and trees stand అక్కడ, "there"; the boys and girls are ఇక్కడ, "here".
*అది మంచి పిల్ల* — the passage calls the child మంచి, "good".

questions.stem: Which words in the passage are **plural**?
questions.explanation: *అబ్బాయిలు* and *కుక్కలు* add -లు plainly; *ఇళ్ళు* is the plural of ఇల్లు with its stem changed. *ఇల్లు* itself, in *ఇది నా ఇల్లు*, is singular — and it is the one that looks plural, ending in -లు already.

questions.stem: The passage speaks of four groups: the boys and girls, the child, the dogs and trees, and the houses. How many of the four are grammatically **non-masculine**?
questions.explanation: Three: the child, the dogs and trees, and the houses. Only the boys and girls together are masculine, because in the plural every person shares one gender regardless of sex — the child, taken alone, does not.
